A restaurant has a 3.9-star average from online reviews. The owner insists most guests love the place. Can both be true?

Easily, because online reviews are not a sample of guests — they are a sample of guests who post reviews, and posting is driven by extremes. Review distributions are famously J-shaped: a pile of 5-star reviews, a pile of 1-star reviews, and a thin middle. The guest who had a perfectly fine 4-star evening rarely feels moved to write anything.

Do the arithmetic on a plausible mix: if 70% of reviewers give 5 stars, 5% give 4, 5% give 3, 5% give 2, and 15% give 1, the mean is 0.7 x 5 + 0.05 x 4 + 0.05 x 3 + 0.05 x 2 + 0.15 x 1 = 3.5 + 0.2 + 0.15 + 0.1 + 0.15 = 4.1 — and that is among reviewers, who already overrepresent the furious. If only 1 in 20 guests reviews, and unhappy guests review at several times the rate of happy ones, the silent majority can be quite satisfied while the visible average sulks below 4.

The owner's error would be the opposite one: reviews do surface real operational problems, and the themes in the 1-star pile are worth reading. But the star average measures reviewer sentiment, not guest satisfaction, and treating it as a census is a category error.
There is a famous World War II story about engineers examining bullet holes in returning bombers to decide where to add armor. Tell it, and name the bias it teaches.

Analysts mapped the bullet holes on bombers that made it back to base: holes clustered on the fuselage and wings, with few around the engines and cockpit. The intuitive move was to armor the holed areas. The statistician Abraham Wald argued the opposite: armor the places with no holes. The returning planes were a biased sample — the ones hit in the engines and cockpit never came home to be counted. The missing holes marked the fatal locations; the visible holes marked hits a plane could survive.

The bias is survivorship bias: drawing conclusions from the subset that made it through a filter, when the filter is related to what you are studying. The data you cannot see is the data that matters.

It recurs everywhere: studying successful companies to learn what causes success (the failures used the same habits), fund performance averages that omit dead funds, 'what do long-lived people eat' studies that cannot interview the dead. Wald's question is the universal antidote: what am I not seeing, and is the reason I am not seeing it connected to my conclusion?

A mall intercept survey interviewed shoppers about spending habits. Age mix of the sample: 18-29: 45%, 30-44: 30%, 45-64: 17%, 65+: 8%. The city's adult population: 18-29: 22%, 30-44: 26%, 45-64: 30%, 65+: 22%. The survey reports average monthly retail spending of $410. What should you do with that number?

Distrust it until it is reweighted. Compare the columns: shoppers aged 18–29 are 45% of the sample but only 22% of the population — overrepresented two-to-one, because young adults frequent malls and agree to interviews. Adults 45–64 are 17% of the sample versus 30% of the population, and those 65+ are 8% versus 22% — the older half of the city is largely missing.

Since spending varies strongly with age, an average computed on this mix is an average of the wrong population: $410 describes young mall shoppers, not city adults. The standard fix is weighting — scale each age group's responses so the sample matches the population shares, which would pull the estimate toward the older groups' spending. Weighting works only if the people interviewed within each age band resemble that band generally; mall-intercept samples can still skew within bands (weekday daytime shoppers differ from everyone else).

The general rule: a survey's first table should always be sample composition versus known population composition. If they diverge and the topic correlates with the divergence, the headline number is a draft, not a result.

A study recruits volunteers for a trial of a supplement and finds the supplement group healthier at the end. A critic mentions the 'healthy volunteer effect.' What is that, and why does randomization not fully cure it?

The healthy volunteer effect is the selection that happens before the study starts: people who volunteer for health research are systematically healthier than the general population — they smoke less, exercise more, have better access to care, and are health-conscious enough to sign up for a trial. Recruitment through clinics, gyms, and universities sharpens the skew.

Randomization cures the comparison inside the study: volunteers are split evenly, so the supplement and placebo groups start equivalent, and a difference at the end can be credited to the supplement. What randomization cannot cure is generalization. The effect was estimated on unusually healthy, motivated people. In the general population — sicker, less adherent, taking other medications — the supplement may work less, differently, or not at all. Internal validity is protected; external validity is not.

This is why trial results so often disappoint at rollout, and why the first question about any study is 'who was in it?' A result is always, silently, a result about its sample. Extending it to everyone else is an argument, not a given.
A research firm surveyed landline owners and reports that 'most households barely use streaming services.' What is the flaw?

The sampling frame excludes exactly the people most likely to stream. Households that rely on streaming tend to cut the cord entirely — no landline, often no cable. A landline directory in this decade reaches an older, less digital slice of the population and structurally cannot reach the cord-cutters whose behavior is the subject of the study. The survey did not find that households barely stream; it found that landline-owning households barely stream, which was nearly true by definition.

This is coverage error: the list you sample from does not cover the population you claim to describe. It poisoned the famous 1936 election poll (lists built from phone and car owners during the Depression) and it poisons modern versions constantly — surveying customers by email about digital exclusion, or app users about app usability.

The fix is to choose the frame to match the claim: if the claim is about households, the frame must be able to reach streaming-only households too — address-based sampling or mobile numbers. A survey can only speak for the people its frame could have reached.
Our employee survey response rate jumped from 30% to 70% after we offered a prize draw for responding, and the results got noticeably more negative. Did morale actually fall?

Probably not — the measuring instrument changed, not the workforce. At a 30% response rate, surveys hear disproportionately from the engaged: people who feel connected, trust the process, and expect to be heard tend to answer without being bribed. The incentive pulled in the other 40% — the indifferent, the busy, and the disaffected who previously could not be bothered. Their more negative answers were always there; they were just missing from the earlier data.

This is why comparing survey waves with different response rates is treacherous: any trend mixes real change with composition change. The 70% wave is likely the more truthful picture of the whole workforce, and the 30% wave was the flattering one.

Good practice: report response rates alongside results, keep methodology constant across waves when trends matter, and when response jumps, compare the early responders (who resemble the old sample) with the late ones to estimate how much of the shift is composition. Morale may also have fallen — but this evidence cannot show it, because the ruler changed length mid-measurement.
A polling firm interviews homeowners and concludes 'the public thinks rents are affordable.' Two problems, please.

Problem one: the sample excludes the population most affected by the question. Renters — the people who actually pay rent and would have the strongest views on its affordability — had zero chance of being interviewed. Surveying homeowners about rent affordability is like surveying drivers about bus service: the respondents are structurally insulated from the thing being judged. Homeowners may even benefit from high rents if they own rental property.

Problem two: even the homeowners reached are those who answer polls, a group that skews older and more settled than homeowners generally.

The deeper lesson is that the population in the conclusion ('the public') must match the population in the sample. Every survey silently answers a narrower question than its headline: this one answered 'what do reachable homeowners think about a cost they do not pay?' Headlines inherit the sample's limits whether they acknowledge them or not.

A company invited 2,000 employees to an anonymous survey; 240 responded (12%). Among respondents, 68% approve of the new policy. Leadership wants to say 'employees approve.' Using worst-case bounds, show what the data actually establishes about all 2,000 employees.

Almost nothing, and the bounds prove it. Approving respondents: 68% of 240 = about 163 people. The other 1,760 employees are unknown.

Best case: every nonrespondent approves. Then approval is (163 + 1,760)/2,000 = 1,923/2,000 = 96.2%.
Worst case: no nonrespondent approves. Then approval is 163/2,000 = 8.2%.

So the survey establishes that true approval lies somewhere between 8% and 96% — a range so wide it excludes almost no possibility. The 68% figure is not wrong; it is a statement about the 240 who answered, silently dressed as a statement about 2,000.

Real nonresponse is rarely worst-case in either direction, but the burden is on the claimant to narrow the range: compare respondents to the workforce on known attributes, or intensively follow up a small random sample of nonrespondents to estimate where they stand. Until then, 'employees approve' is an hypothesis wearing a percentage as a costume.
A poll says Candidate A has 52% support with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. Candidate B has 48%. The headline says 'A leads.' What does the fine print actually allow us to say?

That A is probably ahead, but a tie or a small B lead cannot be ruled out. The margin of error means A's true support is plausibly anywhere in 49% to 55%, and B's in 45% to 51%. The intervals overlap, and configurations like A 49.5%, B 50.5% are consistent with the data.

Two refinements matter. First, the margin of error describes sampling noise only — it assumes the poll sampled randomly and people answered honestly; it says nothing about likely-voter modeling or late swings, which cause most real polling misses. Second, for the gap between candidates the relevant uncertainty is larger than one margin of error suggests, because both numbers wobble; a 4-point lead with a ±3 margin is not a statistically clear lead.

The honest headline is 'A edges ahead in a race within the margin of error.' It sells fewer papers and survives contact with election day far more often.
Explain what a 95% confidence interval really means, because everyone in my office defines it as 'there is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval.'

Your office's definition is the natural one, and under the standard (frequentist) machinery it is not the sanctioned one. The true value is fixed, not random — it is either in this particular interval or it is not, and no probability attaches to it after the data is in.

The 95% is a property of the procedure across hypothetical repetitions: if you reran the study many times and built an interval each time by the same recipe, 95% of those intervals would capture the true value. The confidence is in the method's long-run reliability, like trusting a scale that is right 95% of the time — without being able to certify this particular weighing.

Practically, the distinction rarely changes decisions, and many statisticians speak the office dialect loosely. It matters at the edges: it stops you from saying '95% chance the drug works' when the interval just excludes zero, and it explains why one interval in twenty simply misses, with no one having made an error. If you truly want a probability statement about the parameter, Bayesian credible intervals provide one — at the price of stating a prior.

Two polls measure the same mayor's approval in the same week. Poll 1: 300 respondents, 54% approve. Poll 2: 1,200 respondents, 54% approve. Using the rule of thumb that margin of error is about 1/sqrt(n), compare what each poll establishes.

Same headline number, very different information. Poll 1: 1/sqrt(300) = 1/17.3 = 0.058, so the margin of error is about ±5.8 points. True approval plausibly sits between about 48% and 60% — the poll cannot even rule out that a minority approves.

Poll 2: 1/sqrt(1200) = 1/34.6 = 0.029, about ±2.9 points. The plausible range is roughly 51% to 57% — majority approval is fairly secure.

Quadrupling the sample only halved the margin: precision grows with the square root of n, which is why polls cluster around 1,000 respondents — beyond that, extra interviews buy little precision for their cost. The other moral: a percentage without its sample size is half a fact. '54% approve' from n = 300 and from n = 1,200 are different claims wearing the same costume.
A national poll reports a margin of error of ±3 points, and then breaks out results for voters aged 18-29 showing our candidate ahead by 6. The campaign celebrates the youth lead. What is the catch?

The ±3 applies to the full sample, not to the slice. Margin of error scales with 1/sqrt(n) for the group actually being described. If the poll interviewed 1,200 people and only 90 of them were aged 18–29, the subgroup's margin is about 1/sqrt(90) = 0.105 — plus or minus 10.5 points. A 6-point 'lead' inside a ±10.5-point fog is not a lead; it is a shrug.

News reports almost never print subgroup margins, so the smallest, noisiest slices generate the most dramatic headlines — this demographic loves us, that region hates us — and most of them are noise with a narrative attached. The pattern is worse when someone scans twenty subgroups for the one that looks interesting: the most extreme subgroup is extreme partly by selection.

Rule of thumb: the smaller the subgroup, the bigger the error bars, and any subgroup claim should be quoted with its own n. If the campaign wants a youth number worth celebrating, it has to pay for a youth sample.

A trial of a new migraine drug reports: average reduction in monthly migraine days = 6 days versus placebo, 95% confidence interval from -2 to +14 days. The press release headline: 'New drug cuts migraines by 6 days.' Give the honest interpretation.

The headline reports the point estimate and hides the story, which is the interval. The data is consistent with effects ranging from the drug being slightly worse than placebo (-2) to dramatically better (+14). Zero — no effect at all — sits comfortably inside the interval, so at the conventional standard this trial does not establish that the drug works.

That is not the same as establishing that it does not work. The interval is wide, meaning the trial was small or migraine counts are highly variable; a real benefit of several days remains entirely plausible. The honest summary is 'the estimate is +6 days, but with this sample the true effect could be anywhere from negligible to large; a bigger trial is needed.'

Notice how different that is from a result like +6 with an interval of +4 to +8, which would support the headline. Point estimates without intervals are marketing copy. The interval is the result; the point is just its midpoint.
Two candidates' approval intervals overlap: A is 50% ± 4, B is 46% ± 4. A pundit says overlapping confidence intervals prove the race is tied. Is that right?

No — overlap of two intervals is a weaker condition than no significant difference, and using it as a tie-detector misfires in both directions.

The uncertainty that matters is the uncertainty of the difference, and it is not computed by eyeballing whether two bars touch. When both estimates come from the same poll, they are linked: every respondent who leaves A lands somewhere, often with B, so the gap between them can be estimated more precisely than the overlap suggests. A 4-point gap can be statistically meaningful even while the individual intervals overlap substantially.

Conversely, pundits also err the other way, treating any gap wider than the margin as decisive when the margin quoted was for a single percentage.

The correct procedure is to compute the confidence interval for the difference itself and see whether it includes zero. Rules of thumb about overlapping bars are a visual shortcut with known failure modes — acceptable for a first glance, unacceptable as a verdict on a close race.
A phone maker advertises battery life of 'up to 20 hours.' A review site measured 14 to 19 hours across testers, averaging 16.5. How should a buyer think about these numbers?

As an interval problem, not a promise problem. 'Up to 20 hours' is the best case under the lightest use — a supremum, not an expectation. The review's spread, 14 to 19 hours, is what real variation looks like: battery life depends on screen brightness, signal strength, apps, and battery age, so any single number is a fiction averaged over different lives.

The buyer's useful summary is the range and the middle: expect roughly 16 to 17 hours of typical use, plan around 14 if you are a heavy user. That is exactly the mindset confidence intervals teach — the honest answer to 'how long does it last?' is a distribution, not a point.

Manufacturers quote the supremum because it is the only number that is both technically defensible and large. Whenever you see 'up to' in front of a number — speeds, battery, savings — translate it as 'the best anyone ever measured,' and go find the interval before deciding.

University admissions data. Department A: men 80 admitted of 100 applicants (80%), women 18 of 20 (90%). Department B: men 4 of 20 (20%), women 30 of 100 (30%). A report claims the university favors men. Examine the claim with the totals.

Within each department, women are admitted at a higher rate: 90% vs 80% in Department A, and 30% vs 20% in Department B. Now pool the data. Men: (80 + 4)/(100 + 20) = 84/120 = 70%. Women: (18 + 30)/(20 + 100) = 48/120 = 40%. The totals reverse the story — this is Simpson's paradox.

The mechanism is application patterns. Department A is easy to enter and Department B is highly selective. Men applied mostly to the easy department (100 of their 120 applications), women mostly to the hard one (100 of their 120). Each group's overall rate is a weighted average dominated by where they applied, so the pooled comparison measures application choices more than admission decisions.

This mirrors a famous real case at UC Berkeley in the 1970s, where pooled data suggested bias against women and department-level data dissolved it. The lesson is not that pooled numbers always lie — it is that an aggregate can reverse every subgroup, so a claim about fairness must be checked at the level where decisions are actually made. Here, the departments decide, and at that level the claim fails.

Two hospitals report surgical success rates. Hospital A: mild cases 95 of 100 succeed (95%), severe cases 120 of 300 (40%). Hospital B: mild cases 270 of 300 (90%), severe cases 30 of 100 (30%). A ranking site lists B as the better hospital. A surgeon says the ranking is backwards. Who is right?

The surgeon, about the comparison — and the ranking site, about the arithmetic. Overall rates: A succeeds in (95 + 120)/400 = 215/400 = 53.75%. B succeeds in (270 + 30)/400 = 300/400 = 75%. B really does have the higher overall rate.

But A is better for every kind of patient: 95% vs 90% for mild cases, 40% vs 30% for severe ones. The overall gap exists because the hospitals treat different mixes: three quarters of A's patients are severe cases, while three quarters of B's are mild. A's overall rate is dragged down by its harder caseload; B's is floated by its easier one. This is Simpson's paradox in clinical dress.

For the question a patient actually asks — 'given my condition, where are my chances better?' — the stratified rates are the answer, and A wins both. Overall rates are still useful for planning capacity and total outcomes. The error is ranking quality on a number that mostly measures who walks through the door.

Two tutoring programs report pass rates. Junior band: Program P 45 of 50 pass, Program Q 170 of 200 pass. Senior band: Program P 60 of 200 pass, Program Q 12 of 50 pass. The district's summary says Q is far better overall. Check the summary band by band and overall.

Band by band: Junior — P: 45/50 = 90%; Q: 170/200 = 85%. P is better. Senior — P: 60/200 = 30%; Q: 12/50 = 24%. P is better again.

Overall: P: (45 + 60)/(50 + 200) = 105/250 = 42%. Q: (170 + 12)/(200 + 50) = 182/250 = 72.8%. The district's summary is arithmetically correct and substantively wrong — Simpson's paradox.

The trick is enrollment mix. The junior band passes easily and Q's students are concentrated there (200 of 250). The senior band is hard and P carries most of it (200 of 250). Each program's overall rate is mostly a statement about which band its students sit in. If you are choosing a program for a specific child, the band rates are the only honest comparison, and P wins both. If the district wants one number, it should standardize: apply each program's band rates to a common enrollment mix, which removes the composition effect the summary is currently reporting as quality.

Player X hit .400 in the first half of the season and .200 in the second. Player Y hit .300 in the first half and .190 in the second. X beat Y in both halves, yet the season stats show Y with the higher batting average. The at-bats: first half X had 100, Y had 300; second half X had 300, Y had 100. Verify the season averages and explain.

Verify X: first half 0.400 x 100 = 40 hits; second half 0.200 x 300 = 60 hits. Season: 100 hits in 400 at-bats = 0.250. Verify Y: first half 0.300 x 300 = 90 hits; second half 0.190 x 100 = 19 hits. Season: 109 hits in 400 at-bats = 0.2725, about .273. Y really does finish higher despite losing both halves.

The mechanism is weighting. A season average is not the average of the half averages; it is total hits over total at-bats, so each half counts in proportion to its at-bats. X's good half was his small half (100 at-bats) and his bad half was his big one (300). Y's pattern is the reverse: his better half carries 300 at-bats of weight.

This is Simpson's paradox in its purest form, and it has decided real batting-title arguments. Whenever a rate is built from subgroups of different sizes, the aggregate can contradict every subgroup — and the aggregate is not the 'real' answer, just a differently weighted one. Report the halves alongside the season line.

Our ad platform report: Campaign A converts at 30% on mobile (90 of 300) and 10% on desktop (100 of 1,000). Campaign B converts at 28% on mobile (280 of 1,000) and 9% on desktop (27 of 300). The platform's summary ranks B far ahead overall. Our analyst says A is actually better. Resolve it.

Both are describing the same table; the analyst is answering the better question. Overall: A converts (90 + 100)/(300 + 1,000) = 190/1,300 = 14.6%. B converts (280 + 27)/(1,000 + 300) = 307/1,300 = 23.6%. The platform's summary is arithmetically right.

But A beats B on each device separately: mobile 30% vs 28%, desktop 10% vs 9%. B's overall lead is entirely composition: 1,000 of B's 1,300 impressions are on mobile, the high-converting device, while 1,000 of A's 1,300 are on desktop, where everyone converts poorly. B did not perform better; B was shown to a luckier mix of audiences. Simpson's paradox again.

If you are deciding which campaign's creative and targeting work better, compare within devices — A wins. If you are forecasting total conversions from running B exactly as currently distributed, the 23.6% is the relevant number. The professional fix is to report both, and to standardize when comparing: apply each campaign's device rates to the same impression mix. Ranking campaigns on raw overall rates rewards whoever bought the favorable mix, not whoever made the better ad.

A headline warns: 'Common food additive DOUBLES cancer risk!' The underlying study: among 10,000 people not consuming the additive, 1 developed the cancer over a decade; among 10,000 consumers, 2 did. Present this honestly.

Both framings describe the same table. Relative risk: 2 versus 1 per 10,000 — the risk doubled, so the headline is technically accurate. Absolute risk: consumption is associated with an increase from 0.01% to 0.02% over a decade — one additional case per 10,000 consumers. For an individual deciding whether to worry, the second framing is the informative one.

Relative risks sound alarming precisely when the base rate is tiny, because doubling almost-nothing is still almost-nothing. The same trick in reverse minimizes real dangers: a rise from 20% to 30% can be reported as 'only 10 points' instead of a 50% relative increase.

Honest reporting gives all three numbers: the relative change, the absolute rates, and the denominator with its time window. 'Doubles your risk' with no base rate is a headline designed to frighten; 'one extra case per 10,000 people per decade' is the same fact designed to inform. Also worth adding: with counts of 1 and 2, this difference is far inside statistical noise — a fact neither framing mentioned.

A beach town's press release announces 'shark attacks up 300% this summer!' Last summer there was 1 attack; this summer there were 4. Lifeguards say the beach is about as safe as ever. Who is misleading whom?

The press release is using true arithmetic to create a false impression; the lifeguards have the better of it. The percent increase is real: (4 - 1)/1 = 300%. But percentage changes on tiny counts are explosively unstable — one more or fewer attack swings the figure by 100 points. Going from 1 to 4 events is a change of 3 incidents in a town with perhaps hundreds of thousands of swimmer-days; the underlying risk per swim barely moved, and counts this small fluctuate randomly year to year even with a constant risk.

This is denominator neglect: the brain hears '300%' as a large quantity of danger and skips the base. Honest reporting of rare events uses counts and exposure: '4 attacks this summer versus 1 last summer, over an estimated 2 million swimmer-days.' Rates per million swims would let readers compare across years and towns.

Rule of thumb: whenever a percentage change is quoted for a rare event, ask for the raw counts. If the counts are single digits, the percentage is decoration.

A school has two classes. Class 1: 10 students, average score 80. Class 2: 30 students, average score 70. The principal averages the two class averages and reports a school average of 75. Correct this.

The school average is 72.5, not 75. Averaging the averages treats the two classes as equal halves of the school, but Class 2 has three times the students.

Go back to totals. Class 1 total points: 10 x 80 = 800. Class 2 total points: 30 x 70 = 2,100. School total: 2,900 points over 40 students: 2900/40 = 72.5.

The principal's 75 is the unweighted mean of group means — valid only when the groups are the same size. The correct combination weights each group's mean by its count, which is just a roundabout way of adding up all the individuals. This error is everywhere: averaging branch growth rates, department satisfaction scores, and per-country statistics as if each unit counted equally regardless of how many people it contains. When you combine averages, always ask: averages of how many?

A fund's annual returns for five years: +20%, -10%, +30%, -5%, +15%. The factsheet says 'average annual return: 10%.' An investor who put in $10,000 at the start wants to know what actually happened to the money.

The factsheet's 10% is the arithmetic mean: (20 - 10 + 30 - 5 + 15)/5 = 50/5 = 10%. It is also not what the investor earned.

Compound the returns: $10,000 x 1.20 = $12,000; x 0.90 = $10,800; x 1.30 = $14,040; x 0.95 = $13,338; x 1.15 = $15,338.70. The money grew by a factor of 1.5339 over five years. The annualized (geometric) return is 1.5339^(1/5) - 1 = 8.9% per year.

Had the fund truly returned a steady 10% a year, the investor would have 10,000 x 1.1^5 = $16,105 — about $766 more. The gap between 10% arithmetic and 8.9% geometric is volatility drag: losses hurt more than equal gains help, because a loss shrinks the base the next gain acts on. Factsheets are not lying about the arithmetic mean; they are answering a question no investor actually has. The only average that describes compounded money is the geometric one.
At the roulette table, red has come up 8 times in a row. Half the table is betting black because 'it is due.' Evaluate their reasoning.

It is the gambler's fallacy: the wheel has no memory. Each spin is independent, so after eight reds the probability of black on the next spin is exactly what it always is — 18/38 on an American wheel, about 47.4%, with green zeros taking the rest. The wheel is not keeping score and owes nobody a correction.

The confusion comes from a true fact applied at the wrong scale. Over thousands of spins, the proportion of reds does settle near 50% — but it settles by dilution, as the early streak becomes a negligible share of a huge total, not by compensation. The universe does not send extra blacks to balance the books; it just buries the streak in more data.

Where streaks are genuinely surprising is before the fact: the chance that the next 8 spins are all red is (18/38)^8, well under 1%. But once the streak has happened, its cost is sunk — every specific sequence of 8 outcomes was equally improbable in advance. Betting black now is no smarter than betting red; the only consistent winner at the table is the zero.

Unemployment in a region: 5.0% last year, 6.0% this year. One headline says 'unemployment up 1%.' Another says 'unemployment up 20%.' A third says 'unemployment up one point.' Sort out which are right.

The third headline is the clean one. The rate rose by 1 percentage point: 6.0 - 5.0 = 1.0.

The second headline is also arithmetically defensible: the relative increase is (6.0 - 5.0)/5.0 = 20%. The rate itself grew by a fifth.

The first headline, 'up 1%,' is the muddle to avoid: it blurs the two, and most readers will hear it as the smallest possible change. Percent and percentage point are different units. A change in something already measured in percent must be reported in points (the absolute difference) or as a relative percent change, with the wording making clear which.

The stakes are real: an interest rate rising from 2% to 3% is +1 point and +50% relative — a borrower hears those very differently, and both are true. Honest writers pick the point change for rates and add the relative figure when it matters; dishonest ones pick whichever serves the story.

A team measures a web page's load time five times before a change: [2.4, 2.6, 2.5, 2.7, 2.5] seconds, and five times after: [2.2, 2.4, 2.3, 2.5, 2.3] seconds. They claim 'we made the page 8% faster.' Check the claim and its strength.

The arithmetic first. Before: sum 12.7, mean 12.7/5 = 2.54 seconds. After: sum 11.7, mean 11.7/5 = 2.34 seconds. Difference: 0.20 seconds, and 0.20/2.54 = 7.9% — so the '8% faster' claim matches the sample means.

The strength is another matter. Five measurements each is tiny, and the ranges overlap: the slowest 'after' run (2.5) equals a typical 'before' run, and the fastest 'before' (2.4) beats two of the 'after' runs. Load times also vary with network conditions, time of day, and server load, none of which were controlled — if the 'after' runs happened on a quieter afternoon, the improvement may belong to the afternoon.

Verdict: the direction is encouraging and the size is plausible, but this is a pilot measurement, not a result. Thirty-plus runs per condition, interleaved in time rather than blocked before/after, would turn the claim into evidence. Small samples do not make a claim false; they make it a rumor with good posture.
People say 'the average family has 2.3 children' and 'the average person is 5 foot 7 with an average income.' Why do statisticians wince at the idea of the 'average person'?

Because averages are computed one variable at a time, and nobody is average on all of them at once. When the US Air Force measured thousands of pilots on ten body dimensions in the 1950s, expecting to design a cockpit for the average pilot, they found that zero pilots were within the middle range on all ten dimensions — and only a small fraction were average on even three. Designing for the average on each measurement produced a cockpit that fit nobody.

The same illusion runs through social statistics. 'The average family has 2.3 children' describes no family that exists; it is a total divided by a count. Averages also hide shape: an income distribution and a height distribution with the same mean can look nothing alike, and in skewed distributions the mean is not even typical.

The wince is about reification — treating a summary statistic as if it were a person. Averages are tools for totals, budgets, and comparisons. The moment a decision touches an individual — a cockpit, a dose, a curriculum — design for the range and the distribution, not for the fictional average human standing at the center of them.
